title: Jeremiah 1:1–10
context: The book opens in the narrator’s voice with a heading: these are the words of Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, and the LORD’s word came to him in the days of Josiah, and also in the days of Jehoiakim, to the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah and the carrying away of Jerusalem captive in the fifth month. Jeremiah then recounts, in the first person, how the LORD’s word came to him. The LORD says that before he formed Jeremiah in the womb he knew him, that before he was born he sanctified him, and that he has appointed him a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah answers that he does not know how to speak, for he is a child. The LORD tells him not to say that, promises to be with him to rescue him, stretches out his hand and touches Jeremiah’s mouth, and sets him over the nations and kingdoms to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant. The kings named in the heading, and the fifth-month captivity, are also told in 2 Kings 22–25 and in Jeremiah 39 and 52; those accounts should be named without being blended here. Anathoth and the precise modern dating of Josiah’s thirteenth year are best left hedged. The sentence about being known and appointed before birth is first of all a prophetic commission. Both traditions take God’s prior purpose as shared ground. Classical Arminians affirm exhaustive foreknowledge here and are not read as holding that Jeremiah’s future was open or unknown to God. How, if at all, readers connect the verse to individual salvation is already treated in the existing boxes at Romans 8:29, Galatians 1:15, and Ephesians 1:4–5; those notes may be consulted rather than a new contrast being opened on this verse. Isaiah 6 and Galatians 1:15 may be named as other call texts, without harmonizing the scenes.

verses.text: The words of Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The words of Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin.” The book begins by naming the prophet, his father, his priestly standing, and his town in Benjamin. Anathoth is presented as a place of priests in Benjamin; later or earlier texts sometimes mention a priestly settlement there, but the exact site and the identity of this Hilkiah—whether or not he is the high priest of Josiah’s day—should be left open, because this verse does not settle those questions.

Arminian readers take the heading as a real historical introduction, locating Jeremiah among the priests of Benjamin, not as a later label that weakens the call that follows.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise receive the opening as the book’s own frame: a named priest from Anathoth, in Benjamin, whose words the book will record. The identifications that go beyond the verse remain uncertain and need not be pressed.

Both traditions start from the same heading. There is no party contrast over Jeremiah’s name, family, or town.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to him in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The LORD’s word came to him in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign.” The narrator dates the beginning of the word to Josiah’s thirteenth year. The year is the book’s own marker; converting it to a modern calendar date, or deciding what else in Josiah’s reign it must coincide with, is more than this line states and should be hedged.

Arminian readers hear a real word of the LORD arriving in a dated reign, the start of a ministry in history, not a timeless saying detached from Judah’s kings.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the date as the book’s historical claim: the word came in Josiah’s thirteenth year. Later comparison with 2 Kings 22–25 can be made without forcing this heading to do all the work of that narrative.

Shared ground: the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah in a named king’s reign. The precise modern year is not required in order to read the verse.

verses.text: It came also in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, to the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, the son of Josiah, king of Judah, to the carrying away of Jerusalem captive in the fifth month.
verses.arminianNotes:
The word “came also in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, to the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah,” and “to the carrying away of Jerusalem captive in the fifth month.” The heading stretches the ministry from Josiah through Jehoiakim to Zedekiah and the captivity. 2 Kings 22–25 and Jeremiah 39 and 52 also tell of these kings and of Jerusalem’s fall; they should be named by reference and not merged here into a single blended chronology.

Arminian readers take the span as the book’s claim that Jeremiah’s word ran to the exile, a ministry lived under several kings, not an isolated moment in Josiah’s day.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read a ministry that lasts to the carrying away in the fifth month, and they can consult the later chapters and the Kings narrative without deciding every alignment in this heading.

Both traditions accept the heading’s range. Differences of date or sequence that belong to those later accounts are not to be settled, or denied, from this verse alone.

verses.text: Now the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now the LORD’s word came to me, saying,” The voice shifts. The narrator’s heading gives way to Jeremiah’s own report: the word came to him, and he will tell what was said. The speaker of the call scene is Jeremiah, recounting the LORD’s speech.

Arminian readers take the first-person turn as Jeremiah’s testimony to a word he actually received, the start of the commission, not a later fiction placed in his mouth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear Jeremiah as the witness of the call. The word is the LORD’s, reported by the prophet, and the verse is a simple opening, not yet the content of the charge.

Shared ground: from this line forward, Jeremiah is telling how the LORD spoke to him. There is no party contrast over the change of person.

verses.text: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you. Before you were born, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you. Before you were born, I sanctified you. I have appointed you a prophet to the nations.” The LORD’s first word to Jeremiah is a commission. The LORD knew him, set him apart, and appointed him a prophet to the nations before birth. That prior purpose is shared ground. Classical Arminians affirm that God knew Jeremiah exhaustively before he was formed, not that the future was open or unknown to God. Readers sometimes ask how this verse relates to individual salvation; the sentence itself is about a prophetic appointment. The existing boxes at Romans 8:29, Galatians 1:15, and Ephesians 1:4–5 already treat foreknowledge, a call from the womb, and election, and should be consulted rather than restated here.

Arminian readers therefore keep the verse first of all as the call of a prophet, while allowing that some will compare Galatians 1:15 as a later vocational text, without blending the two scenes or turning this line into a general decree of who will be saved.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the verse as prophetic commission first. They may gladly hear God’s prior knowledge and setting-apart as of a piece with his sovereign purpose, and some will compare Galatians 1:15, where God’s good pleasure and call are said to precede Paul’s work. Even so, this line names a prophet to the nations, and the existing boxes at Romans 8:29, Galatians 1:15, and Ephesians 1:4–5 already discuss foreknowledge and election. Those notes can be read; a new contrast need not be opened here.

Shared ground: God knew, formed, sanctified, and appointed Jeremiah before birth. The verse is about that commission.

verses.text: Then I said, “Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I don’t know how to speak; for I am a child.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Then Jeremiah said, “Ah, Lord GOD! Behold, I don’t know how to speak; for I am a child.” Jeremiah answers the commission with a protest: he does not know how to speak, and he calls himself a child. The word may mean youth, inexperience, or both; the verse does not give his age, and that should not be invented.

Arminian readers hear a real reluctance, a man who feels unready for the sending, not a staged refusal that was never meant. The protest is honest, and the LORD will answer it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the protest as Jeremiah’s own word: he feels unequal to speech and names himself a child. The following verses will show the LORD overruling the objection without treating the fear as a fiction.

Both traditions read a genuine hesitation before the call. There is no party contrast over the meaning of “child” beyond the need to hedge his exact age.

verses.text: But the LORD said to me, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for you must go to whomever I send you, and you must say whatever I command you.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Don’t say, ‘I am a child;’ for you must go to whomever I send you, and you must say whatever I command you.” The objection is not allowed to stand. Jeremiah is to go where he is sent and to say what he is commanded. The sending and the speech are bound together; he is not left to invent the message.

Arminian readers hear a real charge that Jeremiah can obey or resist, a command that takes his protest seriously and then directs him, not a mere announcement that his will cannot be otherwise.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same command as the LORD’s effective word to his prophet: Jeremiah must go and must speak as he is sent. The emphasis falls on the LORD’s right to send and to command, without denying that Jeremiah is addressed as a man who is to rise and speak.

Shared ground: the prophet’s youth or inexperience is not an excuse, and the words he is to speak are the LORD’s.

verses.text: Don’t be afraid because of them, for I am with you to rescue you,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Don’t be afraid because of them, for I am with you to rescue you,” says the LORD. The “them” looks ahead to those Jeremiah will face; the promise is presence and rescue, not a claim that no one will oppose him. The same pledge will be heard again at the end of the chapter.

Arminian readers take the “Don’t be afraid” as a real encouragement addressed to a man who can be afraid, and the promise “I am with you to rescue you” as the LORD’s faithful presence, which Jeremiah is to trust as he goes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also receive a real promise of the LORD’s presence and rescue. The command not to fear rests on what the LORD will be and do, not on Jeremiah’s natural courage.

Both traditions share the pledge. It does not mean that the ministry will be easy, only that the LORD will be with him to rescue him.

verses.text: Then the LORD stretched out his hand and touched my mouth. Then the LORD said to me, “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then the LORD stretched out his hand and touched my mouth.” Then he said, “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.” The call is sealed by a touch and by a gift of words. Isaiah 6 also tells of a mouth touched in a commission scene; that parallel may be named without treating the two accounts as the same event or the same ritual.

Arminian readers hear the LORD actually putting his words in Jeremiah’s mouth, a gift that equips the prophet to speak, not a cancellation of Jeremiah as the one who must still arise and say them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the touch and the saying as the LORD’s act: the words in the mouth are God’s words, given so that the prophet speaks what he is given. Comparison with Isaiah 6, if made, should not flatten either scene.

Shared ground: the message is the LORD’s, placed in Jeremiah’s mouth. The verse does not require a party contrast over the manner of the touch.

verses.text: Behold, I have today set you over the nations and over the kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Behold, I have today set you over the nations and over the kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.” The appointment is “today” and its scope is nations and kingdoms. The six verbs describe what the prophetic word will do, in judgment and in restoration, not a claim that Jeremiah himself rules as a king.

Arminian readers take the setting-over as the authority of the word Jeremiah is given, a commission that will meet real nations who may hear or refuse, and that includes building and planting as well as tearing down.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read an authority given with the word: God sets his prophet over nations and kingdoms for uprooting and for planting. The verbs are the LORD’s work through the word he has put in Jeremiah’s mouth.

Shared ground: the commission is international in scope and holds both judgment and hope. The verse is not a cue to rearrange later oracles against the nations.
